claim: The study investigated genomic imprinting in the cerebellum using a newly developed Bayesian statistical model (BRAIM).
source: Here we investigate genomic imprinting in the cerebellum using a newly developed Bayesian statistical model that provides unprecedented transcript-level resolution.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The study uncovered 160 imprinted transcripts in the cerebellum.
source: We uncover 160 imprinted transcripts, including 41 novel and independently validated imprinted genes.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: 41 novel imprinted genes were identified and independently validated.
source: We uncover 160 imprinted transcripts, including 41 novel and independently validated imprinted genes.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Many genes exhibit parentally biased rather than monoallelic expression.
source: Strikingly, many genes exhibit parentally biased—rather than monoallelic—expression, with different magnitudes according to age, organ, and brain region.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a key observation.

claim: Parental bias varies according to age, organ, and brain region.
source: Strikingly, many genes exhibit parentally biased—rather than monoallelic—expression, with different magnitudes according to age, organ, and brain region.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a key observation.

claim: Developmental changes in parental bias and overall gene expression are strongly correlated.
source: Developmental changes in parental bias and overall gene expression are strongly correlated, suggesting combined roles in regulating gene dosage.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Brain-specific deletion of the paternal allele of Bcl-x results in loss of specific neuron types.
source: Finally, brain-specific deletion of the paternal, but not maternal, allele of the paternally-biased Bcl-x, (Bcl2l1) results in loss of specific neuron types, supporting the functional significance of parental biases.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as an experimental finding.

claim: Brain-specific deletion of the maternal allele of Bcl-x does not result in loss of specific neuron types.
source: Finally, brain-specific deletion of the paternal, but not maternal, allele of the paternally-biased Bcl-x, (Bcl2l1) results in loss of specific neuron types, supporting the functional significance of parental biases.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as an experimental finding.

claim: Genomic imprinting is a unique and long lasting form of epigenetic inheritance that relies on chromatin modifications established in the parental germ lines.
source: Genomic imprinting is a unique and long lasting form of epigenetic inheritance that relies on chromatin modifications or 'imprints' established in the parental germ lines and maintained in cells of the developing and adult organism, resulting in the differential expression of the maternally- or the paternally-inherited allele (Bartolomei and Ferguson-Smith, 2011).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: A substantial number of imprinted genes exhibit biased expression from one of the parental alleles in at least some tissues.
source: Although expression differences between parental alleles are commonly assumed to be all-to-none, a substantial number of imprinted genes have been shown to exhibit a biased expression from one of the parental alleles in at least some tissues (Dao et al., 1998; Lewis et al., 2004; Khatib, 2007; Babak et al., 2008; Menheniott et al., 2008; Tierling et al., 2009; Gregg et al., 2010; Gregg, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Imprinted genes play key roles during embryonic development.
source: Imprinted genes have been shown to play key roles during embryonic development (Cleaton et al., 2014), in the placenta (Tunster et al., 2013), and more recently, in the developing and adult brain (Wilkinson et al., 2007; Keverne, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Imprinted genes play key roles in the placenta.
source: Imprinted genes have been shown to play key roles during embryonic development (Cleaton et al., 2014), in the placenta (Tunster et al., 2013), and more recently, in the developing and adult brain (Wilkinson et al., 2007; Keverne, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Imprinted genes play key roles in the developing and adult brain.
source: Imprinted genes have been shown to play key roles during embryonic development (Cleaton et al., 2014), in the placenta (Tunster et al., 2013), and more recently, in the developing and adult brain (Wilkinson et al., 2007; Keverne, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Imprinted gene expression is preferentially enriched in brain areas involved in feeding, social, and motivated behaviors.
source: A systematic survey of the expression patterns of known imprinted genes in the brain indicates a preferential enrichment of imprinted gene expression in a subset of brain areas, in particular those involved in feeding, social, and motivated behaviors (Gregg et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Prader-Willi syndrome is caused by loss of paternal expression in the q11-13 region of human chromosome 15.
source: For instance, patients with Prader–Willi syndrome, caused by loss of paternal expression in the q11-13 region of human chromosome 15, display abnormal development, hyperphagia, mental retardation, and volatile behavior (Peters, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Patients with Prader-Willi syndrome display abnormal development, hyperphagia, mental retardation, and volatile behavior.
source: For instance, patients with Prader–Willi syndrome, caused by loss of paternal expression in the q11-13 region of human chromosome 15, display abnormal development, hyperphagia, mental retardation, and volatile behavior (Peters, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of maternal expression in the q11-13 region of human chromosome 15.
source: In contrast, Angelman syndrome, which is caused by loss of maternal expression in the same genomic region, results in mental retardation, impaired speech, and an abnormally joyful demeanor (Peters, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Angelman syndrome results in mental retardation, impaired speech, and an abnormally joyful demeanor.
source: In contrast, Angelman syndrome, which is caused by loss of maternal expression in the same genomic region, results in mental retardation, impaired speech, and an abnormally joyful demeanor (Peters, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Birk-Barel mental retardation syndrome is caused by mutations in the human maternally expressed KCNK9 gene.
source: Similarly, Birk-Barel mental retardation syndrome (Barel et al., 2008) is caused by mutations in the human maternally expressed KCNK9 gene, and phenotypes associated with loss of the imprinted genes Grb10, Mest, and Peg3 in the mouse exhibit impairments in specific social behaviors (Lefebvre et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999; Isles et al., 2006; Garfield et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of the imprinted genes Grb10, Mest, and Peg3 in the mouse exhibit impairments in specific social behaviors.
source: Similarly, Birk-Barel mental retardation syndrome (Barel et al., 2008) is caused by mutations in the human maternally expressed KCNK9 gene, and phenotypes associated with loss of the imprinted genes Grb10, Mest, and Peg3 in the mouse exhibit impairments in specific social behaviors (Lefebvre et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999; Isles et al., 2006; Garfield et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Subsets of genes exhibit tissue-specific imprinting.
source: Surprisingly, subsets of genes have been reported to exhibit tissue-specific imprinting, and the whole brain, neurons and certain brain regions emerged as hot spots for such regulation (Albrecht et al., 1997; Gregg et al., 2010; Sato and Stryker, 2010; Prickett and Oakey, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The whole brain, neurons and certain brain regions are hot spots for tissue-specific imprinting regulation.
source: Surprisingly, subsets of genes have been reported to exhibit tissue-specific imprinting, and the whole brain, neurons and certain brain regions emerged as hot spots for such regulation (Albrecht et al., 1997; Gregg et al., 2010; Sato and Stryker, 2010; Prickett and Oakey, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Approximately 100 imprinted genes were identified through initial methods based on differential expression between parthenogenetic and androgenetic embryos.
source: Initial methods to uncover imprinted genes based on the differential expression between parthenogenetic (containing only maternally derived chromosomes) and androgenetic (containing only paternally derived chromosomes) embryos, and subsequent discovery of adjacent imprinted loci within the genome were mainly focused on early developmental stages, and led to the identification of approximately 100 imprinted genes (Kaneko-Ishino et al., 1995; Hagiwara et al., 1997; Morison et al., 2005; Ruf et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Wang et al. (2008) and Babak et al. (2008) used neonatal brains and E9.5 embryos, respectively, in pioneer RNA-seq analyses of mouse hybrids.
source: In pioneer RNA-seq analyses of mouse hybrids, Wang et al. (2008) and Babak et al. (2008) used neonatal brains and E9.5 embryos, respectively, and determined parental biases by testing if the sum of parentally phased reads along a gene significantly deviates from biallelic expression.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: Wang et al. (2008) and Babak et al. (2008) only identified a handful of novel imprinted genes and failed to detect genes known to be imprinted in the profiled tissues.
source: This approach, combined with shallow sequencing, only identified a handful of novel imprinted genes and failed to detect genes known to be imprinted in the profiled tissues.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a critique of prior work.

claim: Gregg et al. (2010) conducted an imprinting study with over 10-fold higher sequencing depth compared to Wang et al. (2008) and Babak et al. (2008).
source: Next, Gregg et al. (2010) conducted an imprinting study at higher resolution by characterizing the preoptic area and prefrontal cortex of adult males and females, and the E15 brain, with an over 10-fold higher sequencing depth compared to the two previous studies.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Gregg et al. (2010) identified a much larger number of novel imprinted gene candidates by testing for deviation from biallelic expression at each single SNP.
source: This experimental design, combined with testing for deviation from biallelic expression of parentally phased reads at each single SNP rather than along an entire gene, resulted with a much larger number of novel imprinted gene candidates.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Most of the novel imprinted candidates from Gregg et al. (2010) were not subject to independent experimental validation.
source: However, most of the novel imprinted candidates were not subject to independent experimental validation.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a critique of prior work.

claim: DeVeale et al. (2012) criticized the use of single SNPs to infer imprinting and the lack of systematic independent validation of Gregg et al. (2010).
source: In turn, DeVeale et al. (2012) criticized the use of single SNPs to infer imprinting and the lack of systematic independent validation of Gregg et al. (2010) as leading to a large and underestimated false discovery rate, and suggested that the vast majority of imprinted genes in mouse were likely already uncovered (DeVeale et al., 2012; Kelsey and Bartolomei, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in motor control and implicated in autism spectrum disorders.
source: We performed a genome-wide screen for imprinted genes in the cerebellum, a brain structure involved in motor control and implicated in autism spectrum disorders (Amaral et al., 2008; Tsai et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014b).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: Cerebellar development occurs largely postnatally.
source: Moreover, unlike other brain structures, cerebellar development occurs largely postnatally, thus providing direct access to key neurodevelopmental processes such as cell proliferation, migration, and synaptogenesis (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: RNA transcripts were sequenced from 48 individual cerebella representing two developmental stages and both sexes.
source: Tissue was dissected from F1 mouse hybrids of Cast/EiJ and C57Bl/6J reciprocal crosses and RNA transcripts were sequenced from 48 individual cerebella representing two developmental stages and both sexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the experimental design.

claim: Half of the cerebella were collected at postnatal day 8 (P8).
source: Half of the cerebella were collected at postnatal day 8 (P8), a period in which newly-born granule cells migrate to the inner granule layer.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the experimental design.

claim: The remaining cerebella samples were collected from adult animals (P60).
source: The remaining samples were collected from adult animals (P60).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the experimental design.

claim: Each age group had equal numbers of males and females.
source: Each age group had equal numbers of males and females.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the experimental design.

claim: The experimental design includes six replicates for each cross, sex, and age combination.
source: Therefore, our experimental design includes six replicates for each cross, sex, and age combination, which enables inference of genomic imprinting across all individuals, while taking into account the effects of the different experimental factors.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the experimental design.

claim: The model was fitted to 49,464 heterozygous autosomal and X-linked transcripts from 31,547 genes.
source: We fitted our model to 49,464 heterozygous autosomal and X-linked transcripts (comprised of 32,399 protein-coding and 17,065 non-coding transcripts, see 'Materials and methods') from 31,547 genes expressed at levels above 0.01 transcripts per million (TPM) units (solid line in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the analysis.

claim: A minimal threshold of 0.01 TPM was chosen because it allows for accurate and independently validated detection of parentally biased genes.
source: A minimal threshold of 0.01 TPM was chosen because it allows for accurate and independently validated detection of parentally biased genes.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the analysis.

claim: The study set PP > 0.95 as the cutoff for calling an effect significant.
source: It also clearly identifies a group of autosomal transcripts with PP > 0.95, which we set as our cutoff for calling an effect significant ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the analysis.

claim: The analysis identifies a clear and substantial effect of strain on expression.
source: Our analysis also identifies a clear and substantial effect of strain on expression, as evidenced by the distribution of PPs when we account for the cross (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A–C).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The effect of strain on expression is most likely due to the divergence of the Cast/EiJ and C57Bl/6J strains in cis-regulatory regions.
source: This is most likely due to the divergence of the Cast/EiJ and C57Bl/6J strains, specifically in cis-regulatory regions of the genes expressed in the cerebellum.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: No autosomal imprinted transcripts with a sex effect with PP above 0.95 were identified.
source: We did not identify autosomal imprinted transcripts with a sex effect with PP above the 0.95 cutoff, indicating that genomic imprinting is sex invariant in the mouse cerebellum.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a finding.

claim: Genomic imprinting is sex invariant in the mouse cerebellum.
source: We did not identify autosomal imprinted transcripts with a sex effect with PP above the 0.95 cutoff, indicating that genomic imprinting is sex invariant in the mouse cerebellum.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: A group of autosomal imprinted transcripts have an age effect with PPs above 0.95.
source: However, a group of autosomal imprinted transcripts were found to have an age effect with PPs above the 0.95 cutoff, indicating age-regulated imprinting (described in more detail below).
evidence: Stated in the results section as a finding.

claim: Two transcripts of the known imprinted Xlr3b gene were detected among X-linked transcripts.
source: Finally, among X-linked transcripts, above the PP cutoff, we detect two transcripts of the known imprinted Xlr3b gene (Davies et al., 2005), and a single transcript from each of two Xlr3b paralogs, Xlr3a and Xlr3c (Supplementary file 1D–F).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: 124 genes represented by 169 transcripts were identified as candidate imprinted genes.
source: Using these criteria, we identified 124 genes represented by 169 transcripts as candidate imprinted genes in our data (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: Stated in the results section as a finding.

claim: 74 of the candidate genes were reported and validated as imprinted in previously published studies.
source: Among these candidates, 74 genes were reported and validated as imprinted in previosuly published studies (Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: 50 candidate genes have not been previously described as imprinted.
source: The remaining 50 genes have not been previously described as imprinted (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Pyrosequencing was used to independently evaluate parental allelic expression bias in all candidate genes.
source: To independently evaluate parental allelic expression bias in all these candidates, we used pyrosequencing, a real-time sequence-by-synthesis approach relying on light emissions after nucleotide incorporation (Wang and Elbein, 2007).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the validation method.

claim: 11 known imprinted genes were tested as positive controls.
source: As positive and negative controls, we tested 11 known imprinted genes and 11 randomly selected genes with no significant parental effects according to our RNA-seq analysis, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the validation method.

claim: 11 randomly selected genes with no significant parental effects were tested as negative controls.
source: As positive and negative controls, we tested 11 known imprinted genes and 11 randomly selected genes with no significant parental effects according to our RNA-seq analysis, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the validation method.

claim: An average of two SNPs per gene were tested in pyrosequencing validations.
source: For each candidate and control gene, we tested an average of two SNPs per gene ('Materials and methods') in 12 individual cerebella dissected from P60 and/or 12 P8 hybrids.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the validation method.

claim: Pyrosequencing data confirmed significant parental effects for 41 of the candidate novel imprinted genes.
source: The pyrosequencing data confirmed significant parental effects for 41 of the candidate novel imprinted genes and the expected significant and non-significant parental effects for all positive and negative controls, respectively (Figure 1C,D and Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1C,D.

claim: A slightly greater number of genes with a paternal bias were observed among imprinted cerebellar genes.
source: Among the imprinted cerebellar genes identified, we observed a slightly greater number of genes with a paternal bias (Figure 1E).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Five genes preferentially express distinct isoforms from both the maternal and paternal alleles.
source: Interestingly, five genes preferentially express distinct isoforms from both the maternal and paternal alleles (Figure 1E and see below).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The distribution of parental biases spans a wide range from weak bias to strong monoallelic expression.
source: The distribution of the parental biases in the 115 novel and known imprinted genes spans a wide range, from a weak bias (just above 50:50%) up to strong monoallelic expression (100:0%).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the data.

claim: The bias distribution follows a bimodal shape at its two extremes.
source: The bias distribution follows a bimodal shape at its two extremes (Figure 1F), with 36 genes displaying weak biases (from slightly above 50:50–60:40%) and 55 genes showing strong biases (90:10–100:0%).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: 36 genes display weak biases (from slightly above 50:50–60:40%).
source: The bias distribution follows a bimodal shape at its two extremes (Figure 1F), with 36 genes displaying weak biases (from slightly above 50:50–60:40%) and 55 genes showing strong biases (90:10–100:0%).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: 55 genes show strong biases (90:10–100:0%).
source: The bias distribution follows a bimodal shape at its two extremes (Figure 1F), with 36 genes displaying weak biases (from slightly above 50:50–60:40%) and 55 genes showing strong biases (90:10–100:0%).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: The weak bias mode is enriched with newly identified imprinted genes.
source: Interestingly, the weak bias mode is enriched with newly identified imprinted genes (yet includes 10 detected known imprinted genes) whereas stronger biases are enriched with known imprinted genes (yet includes 18 newly detected imprinted genes).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the data.

claim: Stronger biases are enriched with known imprinted genes.
source: Interestingly, the weak bias mode is enriched with newly identified imprinted genes (yet includes 10 detected known imprinted genes) whereas stronger biases are enriched with known imprinted genes (yet includes 18 newly detected imprinted genes).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the data.

claim: A strong correspondence (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.91, p-value < 10−16) is found between the biases identified by RNA-seq and pyrosequencing.
source: A strong correspondence (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.91, p-value < 10−16) is found between the biases identified by RNA-seq and pyrosequencing, respectively, thus suggesting high accuracy in their quantification (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The precision of the approach is approximately 93%.
source: Considering 74 known imprinted genes detected in this analysis as true positives, together with 41 newly validated imprinting genes out of 50 novel candidates (altogether represented by 160 transcripts), the precision of our approach is ∼93% and increases the number of identified mouse imprinted genes by ∼30% (from 138 to 179, see Supplementary file 1G, H).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the performance of the method.

claim: The approach increases the number of identified mouse imprinted genes by approximately 30% (from 138 to 179).
source: Considering 74 known imprinted genes detected in this analysis as true positives, together with 41 newly validated imprinting genes out of 50 novel candidates (altogether represented by 160 transcripts), the precision of our approach is ∼93% and increases the number of identified mouse imprinted genes by ∼30% (from 138 to 179, see Supplementary file 1G, H).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the impact of the study.

claim: Fkbp6 shows almost exclusive expression from the paternal allele.
source: A newly detected imprinted gene, Fkbp6, shows almost exclusive expression from the paternal allele, while Ago2 and Nhlrc1 show moderate to weak parental biases, respectively, and Clptm1l is accurately detected as biallelically-expressed.
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Ago2 and Nhlrc1 show moderate to weak parental biases.
source: A newly detected imprinted gene, Fkbp6, shows almost exclusive expression from the paternal allele, while Ago2 and Nhlrc1 show moderate to weak parental biases, respectively, and Clptm1l is accurately detected as biallelically-expressed.
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Clptm1l is accurately detected as biallelically-expressed.
source: A newly detected imprinted gene, Fkbp6, shows almost exclusive expression from the paternal allele, while Ago2 and Nhlrc1 show moderate to weak parental biases, respectively, and Clptm1l is accurately detected as biallelically-expressed.
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Most imprinted genes show a consistent imprinting pattern in all isoforms.
source: Our data suggest that most imprinted genes, including Rian, show a consistent imprinting pattern in all isoforms.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing isoform-specific imprinting.

claim: Isoform-specific imprinting is readily identified by the approach.
source: However, isoform-specific imprinting is readily identified by our approach, and can be seen in two different genomic contexts.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing isoform-specific imprinting.

claim: The H13-Mcts2 locus exhibits isoform-specific imprinting.
source: Our analysis readily identified previously reported cases of genes in which isoforms are subject to such regulation (e.g., the H13-Mcts2 locus, Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Herc3 gene exhibits isoform-specific imprinting with two short transcripts preferentially expressed by the maternal allele.
source: Moreover, it detected additional imprinted transcripts in the Herc3 gene- either or both of two short transcripts (indistinguishable by our sequence data) from a promoter upstream to the large 25 exons-long transcript (Gencode transcript IDs: ENSMUST00000141600.1 and ENSMUST00000122981.1), which are preferentially expressed by the maternal allele (Figure 3C).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: A novel maternally expressed short transcript (791 bp) was detected at the locus of the paternally expressed Mest gene.
source: Interestingly, we detect a novel maternally expressed short transcript (791 bp) (Gencode transcript ID: ENSMUST00000149496.1) at the locus of the paternally expressed Mest gene, whose transcription starts at exon 9, suggesting alternative promoter usage (Figure 3D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The novel short transcript at the Mest locus is presumably a non-coding RNA since no open reading frame could be identified.
source: This transcript is presumably a non-coding RNA since no open reading frame could be identified.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from the data.

claim: 8 of the 10 known cases of isoform-specific imprinting were detected.
source: In total, we detected 8 of the 10 known cases of isoform-specific imprinting (the missing two cases are the short isoform of Cdh15, which is not expressed in the cerebellum, and the long isoform of Blcap, which is not heterozygous in the Cast/EiJ×C57Bl/6J hybrids), and we uncovered additional imprinted isoforms, including a novel example of isoform-specific imprinting in the Mest locus.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: The imprinted status of eight genes expressed at both P8 and P60 changes according to age.
source: Comparison of imprinted gene expression in the cerebellum in adulthood and at P8, a critical milestone of cerebellar development during which granule cells undergo cell division, migration, and synaptogenesis (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012) shows that the imprinted status of eight genes expressed at both P8 and P60 changes according to age (7 genes are exclusively imprinted at P8 and one is exclusively imprinted at P60 Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4A and citations to prior work.

claim: 7 genes are exclusively imprinted at P8.
source: Comparison of imprinted gene expression in the cerebellum in adulthood and at P8, a critical milestone of cerebellar development during which granule cells undergo cell division, migration, and synaptogenesis (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012) shows that the imprinted status of eight genes expressed at both P8 and P60 changes according to age (7 genes are exclusively imprinted at P8 and one is exclusively imprinted at P60 Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: One gene is exclusively imprinted at P60.
source: Comparison of imprinted gene expression in the cerebellum in adulthood and at P8, a critical milestone of cerebellar development during which granule cells undergo cell division, migration, and synaptogenesis (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Hashimoto and Hibi, 2012) shows that the imprinted status of eight genes expressed at both P8 and P60 changes according to age (7 genes are exclusively imprinted at P8 and one is exclusively imprinted at P60 Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: 29 out of 107 imprinted genes exhibit changes in the magnitude of the parental bias according to age.
source: In addition, we observe changes in the magnitude of the parental bias according to age for 29 out of 107 imprinted genes that are expressed at both age groups, with the majority exhibiting a stronger parental bias at P8 than in the adult (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The majority of age-regulated genes exhibit a stronger parental bias at P8 than in the adult.
source: In addition, we observe changes in the magnitude of the parental bias according to age for 29 out of 107 imprinted genes that are expressed at both age groups, with the majority exhibiting a stronger parental bias at P8 than in the adult (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: 34 of the 107 imprinted genes are differentially expressed between P8 and P60.
source: Moreover, analysis of the overall expression level (sum of paternal and maternal allelic expression) reveals that 34 of the 107 imprinted genes are differentially expressed between P8 and P60 (Supplementary file 1A), together with 8 imprinted genes that are exclusively expressed at P8.
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: 8 imprinted genes are exclusively expressed at P8.
source: Moreover, analysis of the overall expression level (sum of paternal and maternal allelic expression) reveals that 34 of the 107 imprinted genes are differentially expressed between P8 and P60 (Supplementary file 1A), together with 8 imprinted genes that are exclusively expressed at P8.
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The majority of the 34 age-regulated genes show higher expression in the developing cerebellum than in the adult.
source: Similar to the parental bias, the majority of the 34 age-regulated genes show higher expression in the developing cerebellum than in the adult (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: 59 imprinted genes (51% of all imprinted genes expressed in the cerebellum) are regulated in either parental bias and/or overall expression level according to developmental stage.
source: Altogether, 59 imprinted genes (51% of all imprinted genes expressed in the cerebellum) are regulated in either parental bias and/or overall expression level according to developmental stage (age effect PP > 0.95).
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: For the majority of age-regulated genes, the highest magnitude of the parental bias and the highest level of expression are observed at P8.
source: For the majority of these genes, the highest magnitude of the parental bias and the highest level of expression are observed at P8, suggesting a potential role for these genes in neurodevelopmental processes.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: The Asb4 gene exhibits highly maternally-biased expression during cerebellar development but is biallelically expressed during adulthood.
source: For instance, the Asb4 gene, which regulates embryonic stem-cell differentiation (Townley-Tilson et al., 2014), exhibits highly maternally-biased expression during cerebellar development but is biallelically expressed during adulthood, which is achieved by a significant decrease in maternal expression and a slight increase in paternal expression (Figure 4F).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4F and citation to prior work.

claim: The Grb10 gene exhibits biallelic expression at P8 but exclusive paternal expression in the adult.
source: The growth suppressor Grb10 gene exhibits biallelic expression at P8 but exclusive paternal expression in the adult resulting from silencing of the maternal allele (Figure 4F).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Zim1 shows a switch in the parental bias from maternal during development to paternal in the adult cerebellum.
source: Interestingly, we observed a switch in the parental bias for the transcription factor Zim1, from maternal during development to paternal in the adult cerebellum due to a reduction in maternal expression level (PP = 1.0), and no change in paternal expression (PP = 0.19) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A novel imprinted locus at the distal end of chromosome 1 exhibits age-dependent regulation.
source: Our analysis uncovered a novel imprinted locus at the distal end of chromosome 1, which exhibits age-dependent regulation.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: The genes Ier5, Mr1, Stx6, and Impar are located side by side within 136 KB and show a maternal bias during cerebellum development but biallelic expression in the adult.
source: The genes Ier5, Mr1, Stx6, and the putative BC034090 gene, which we name here Impar (for Imprinted and Age Regulated) are located side by side within 136 KB and show a maternal bias during cerebellum development but biallelic expression in the adult (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4F,G.

claim: Stx6 has been shown to regulate neuronal migration and the formation of neural processes.
source: Stx6 has been shown to regulate neuronal migration and the formation of neural processes (Kabayama et al., 2008; Tiwari et al., 2011), two events necessary for the integration of granule cells to the cerebellar circuit occurring at the P8 stage.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: The age effects on the magnitude of the parental bias and on the overall expression are positively correlated.
source: Our analysis shows that the age effects on the magnitude of the parental bias and on the overall expression are positively correlated, such that both the magnitude of the parental bias and the overall expression level of imprinted genes tend to increase or decrease together with age (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.33; p-value = 4 × 10−4, Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Age regulated expression or parental bias is achieved either by a significant change in the expression level only of the most highly expressed (preferred) parental allele (19 genes), a significant change in the expression level only of the non-preferred allele (8 genes), or a significant change in the expression levels of both alleles (12 genes).
source: This analysis reveals that age regulated expression or parental bias (age effect PP > 0.95) is achieved either by a significant change in the expression level only of the most highly expressed (preferred) parental allele (PA; 19 genes, aligned along the X-axis in Figure 4E), a significant change in the expression level only of the non-preferred allele (8 genes, aligned along the Y-axis in Figure 4E), or a significant change in the expression levels of both alleles (12 genes, aligned along the diagonal in Figure 4E).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Altering the expression level of the preferred allele is the most common mode through which imprinted genes are regulated according to age.
source: Thus, our data suggest that altering the expression level of the preferred allele is the most common mode through which imprinted genes are regulated according to age (p-value = 0.03; χ2 test), and this allelic regulation changes both the parental bias as well as the overall expression level.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: 106 of the 115 genes found imprinted in the cerebellum (92%) are located within 1 MB of at least one other imprinted gene.
source: Of the 115 genes found imprinted in the cerebellum, 106 (92%) are located within 1 MB of at least one other imprinted gene.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing genomic localization.

claim: 9 genes (8%) are isolated from other known or newly identified imprinted genes.
source: The remaining 9 genes (8%) are isolated from other known or newly identified imprinted genes.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing genomic localization.

claim: 7 of the 41 newly identified imprinted genes (17%) appear isolated in the genome.
source: Moreover, although most newly identified imprinted genes from this study are located within or around known imprinted clusters, 7 of the 41 (17%) appear isolated in the genome (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5A,B.

claim: A substantial number of imprinted genes displaying weak to moderate parental bias localize to the vicinity of imprinted genes showing stronger parental bias.
source: We noticed that a substantial number of imprinted genes displaying weak to moderate parental bias localize to the vicinity of imprinted genes showing stronger parental bias (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Analysis of the magnitude of the parental bias as a function of the distance to the cluster center reveals a statistically significant negative effect (p-value = 1.08 × 10−4).
source: Analysis of the magnitude of the parental bias as a function of the distance to the cluster center reveals a statistically significant negative effect (p-value = 1.08 × 10−4, 'Materials and methods'), supporting a model of decay of parental bias from imprinted cluster centers (Figure 5D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The mean propensity of adjacency of mammalian orthologs of weakly imprinted gene pairs in the mouse is significantly higher than the mean propensity of adjacency of orthologs of all mouse adjacent gene pairs (p-value = 0.007).
source: This analysis reveals that the mean propensity of adjacency of mammalian orthologs of weakly imprinted gene pairs in the mouse (parental biases below 85%) is significantly higher than the mean propensity of adjacency of orthologs of all mouse adjacent gene pairs (p-value = 0.007, Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5F.

claim: The micro-synteny of imprinted clusters is evolutionary conserved.
source: These findings suggest that the micro-synteny of imprinted clusters is evolutionary conserved, thus supporting the idea that the imprinting regulation of mouse genes with weak-to-moderate parental biases is functionally important.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Differential methylation was observed in a region of chromosome 13 immediately downstream of Nhlrc1.
source: For example, differential methylation was observed in a region of chromosome 13 immediately downstream of Nhlrc1 (Xie et al., 2012), a novel paternally-biased gene in our results (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Mutations in Nhlrc1 cause Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in Nhlrc1 cause Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy (Romá-Mateo et al., 2012), a fatal neurological disorder characterized by the presence of massive intracellular inclusions observed in several neuronal cell types across the brain including the cerebellar granule cells.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Differential methylation but not parentally biased expression in the brain was reported within the Actn1 gene at chromosome 12.
source: Differential methylation but not parentally biased expression in the brain was also reported within the Actinin alpha 1 (Actn1) gene at chromosome 12 (Calaway and Domínguez, 2012), which codes for a protein that regulates cytoskeleton interactions with the membrane.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Actn1 is preferentially expressed from the paternal allele in the cerebellum.
source: Our results show that this gene is indeed preferentially expressed from the paternal allele in the cerebellum.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: Fkbp6 displays maternal allele-specific binding of ZFP57.
source: Interestingly, this gene displays maternal allele-specific binding of ZFP57, a DNA-binding protein that specifically binds to the majority of imprinted genes and protects them from demethylation after fertilization (Quenneville et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Pronounced changes of parental bias across genes and tissues were revealed by pyrosequencing quantification.
source: This analysis revealed pronounced changes of parental bias across genes and tissues (Figure 6C,D and Supplementary file 1J, K).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6C,D.

claim: Igf2 is robustly maternally biased in all 16 brain regions tested.
source: Igf2, previously shown to be maternally biased in the adult cortex and preoptic area (Gregg et al., 2010), is indeed confirmed to be robustly maternally biased in all 16 brain regions tested, while it is mainly expressed from the paternal allele in non-brain tissues.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Igf2 is mainly expressed from the paternal allele in non-brain tissues.
source: Igf2, previously shown to be maternally biased in the adult cortex and preoptic area (Gregg et al., 2010), is indeed confirmed to be robustly maternally biased in all 16 brain regions tested, while it is mainly expressed from the paternal allele in non-brain tissues.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Grb10 is paternally biased in the brain and maternally biased in the body.
source: This stands in contrast to Grb10, which is paternally biased in the brain and maternally biased in the body (Charalambous et al., 2003, 2010; Garfield et al., 2011) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: Igf2r is maternally expressed during development and in most adult tissues with the exception of the brain.
source: Igf2r, which exerts a function that is antagonistic to that of the paternally expressed Igf2, has been shown to be maternally expressed during development (Filson et al., 1993; Ludwig et al., 1996) and in most adult tissues with the exception of the brain (Hu et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the parental biases showed three main clades comprising maternally biased genes, paternally biased genes, and genes that are sporadically biased in the brain.
source: Hierarchical clustering of the parental biases of the tested genes showed three main clades comprising maternally biased genes, paternally biased genes, and genes that are sporadically biased in the brain.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the analysis.

claim: Several genes exhibit sharp contrasts in parental bias between the brain and body.
source: Several genes exhibit sharp contrasts in parental bias between the brain and body.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: Ube3a, Trappc9, Bag3, and B3gnt2 are exclusively or nearly exclusively biased in and throughout the brain.
source: This includes genes that are exclusively or nearly exclusively biased in and throughout the brain, such as the maternally-biased Ube3a (Rougeulle et al., 1997), Trappc9, Bag3, and B3gnt2 genes and the paternally-biased Bcl-x long isoform (Bcl-xL), Inpp5f_v2 isoform (Choi et al., 2005), and Begain gene (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: Bcl-xL, Inpp5f_v2 isoform, and Begain are paternally-biased and exclusively or nearly exclusively biased in and throughout the brain.
source: This includes genes that are exclusively or nearly exclusively biased in and throughout the brain, such as the maternally-biased Ube3a (Rougeulle et al., 1997), Trappc9, Bag3, and B3gnt2 genes and the paternally-biased Bcl-x long isoform (Bcl-xL), Inpp5f_v2 isoform (Choi et al., 2005), and Begain gene (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: Hierarchical clustering separates tissues into two main clades, non-brain and brain.
source: Hierarchical clustering also clearly separates tissues into two main clades, non-brain and brain, with parental bias in brain appearing much more consistent and robust.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the analysis.

claim: Parental bias in brain appears much more consistent and robust than in non-brain tissues.
source: Hierarchical clustering also clearly separates tissues into two main clades, non-brain and brain, with parental bias in brain appearing much more consistent and robust.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the analysis.

claim: Ago2, Chrac1, and the long isoform of Trappc9 exhibit a similar pattern of maternal bias across the brain, stronger in the cortex and weaker in the olfactory bulb, hippocampus, and cerebellum.
source: This analysis revealed that Ago2, Chrac1, and the long isoform of Trappc9, which co-localize to an imprinted cluster in the distal end of chromosome 15, exhibit a similar pattern of maternal bias across the brain, stronger in the cortex and weaker in the olfactory bulb, hippocampus, and cerebellum (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 1K).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Copg2 and the short isoform of Mest exhibit a similar pattern of bias to that of genes on the distal end of chromosome 15.
source: Interestingly, Copg2 and the short isoform of Mest, which co-localize near the centromeric region of chromosome 6, exhibit a similar pattern of bias to that of genes on the distal end of chromosome 15 (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 1K).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The brain executes region-specific programs of imprinting involving genes from the same or distinct imprinted clusters.
source: These results suggest that the brain executes region-specific programs of imprinting involving genes from the same or distinct imprinted clusters.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Blcap exhibits a gradual decrease in maternal bias over development consistently across the three analyzed brain regions.
source: For instance, Blcap exhibits a gradual decrease in maternal bias over development consistently across the three analyzed brain regions.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: The switch from maternal to paternal bias of Zim1 during cerebellum development occurs gradually along development in both the cerebellum and cortex, yet is not mirrored in the hypothalamus where maternal bias is strongly maintained into adulthood.
source: In contrast, the switch from maternal to paternal bias of Zim1 during cerebellum development, occurs gradually along development in both the cerebellum and cortex, yet is not mirrored in the hypothalamus where maternal bias is strongly maintained into adulthood.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: The sharp contrast between the parental biases of Igf2 and Grb10 observed across the brain seems to be temporally co-regulated.
source: Moreover, this analysis reveals that the sharp contrast between the parental biases of Igf2 and Grb10, observed across the brain, seems to be temporally co-regulated.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: The switch in the expressed allele for both Igf2 and Grb10 happens earlier in the cortex and hypothalamus than in the cerebellum.
source: The switch in the expressed allele for both genes happens earlier in the cortex and hypothalamus than in the cerebellum, which roughly coincides with the completion of their development (Levitt et al., 1997; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Shimogori et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: The category of programmed cell death (apoptosis) includes eight genes previously shown to exhibit parent-of-origin monoallelic expression, and five genes newly identified as exhibiting parentally biased expression.
source: The category of programmed cell death (apoptosis) includes eight genes previously shown to exhibit parent-of-origin monoallelic expression, and five genes that we have newly identified as exhibiting parentally biased expression (Figure 8A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: The programmed cell death pathway is a prominent target of imprinting.
source: Our data thus uncover the programmed cell death pathway as a prominent target of imprinting.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Most of the maternally-biased genes (Cdkn1c, Kcnk9, Blcap, and Bmf) promote apoptosis.
source: Noticeably, most of the maternally-biased genes (Cdkn1c, Kcnk9, Blcap, and Bmf) promote apoptosis, while most of the paternally-biased genes (Ndn, Peg3, Peg10, Plagl1, and Magel2) inhibit apoptosis.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: Most of the paternally-biased genes (Ndn, Peg3, Peg10, Plagl1, and Magel2) inhibit apoptosis.
source: Noticeably, most of the maternally-biased genes (Cdkn1c, Kcnk9, Blcap, and Bmf) promote apoptosis, while most of the paternally-biased genes (Ndn, Peg3, Peg10, Plagl1, and Magel2) inhibit apoptosis.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: Bcl-x can produce two distinct protein isoforms: the anti-apoptotic Bcl-xL and the pro-apoptotic Bcl-xS.
source: One gene of particular interest is the paternally-biased Bcl-x (Gregg et al., 2010), which can produce two distinct protein isoforms: the anti-apoptotic Bcl-xL and the pro-apoptotic Bcl-xS, translated from two distinct mRNA transcripts (Boise et al., 1993).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citations to prior work.

claim: Bcl-xL is by far the predominant Bcl-x transcript in the brain.
source: Bcl-xL is by far the predominant Bcl-x transcript in the brain (Krajewska et al., 2002), where it exhibits widespread paternally-biased expression (Figure 8B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Bag3 was newly identified as maternally-biased in the brain and biallelic in peripheral tissues.
source: Also of interest is the gene Bag3, which was newly identified by our study as maternally-biased in the brain and biallelic in peripheral tissues (Figure 8B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: The protein products of Bcl-xL and Bag3 interact to prevent the mitochondrial release of factors controlling activation of caspases.
source: However, a suggested function of these proteins, mediated by their mutual interaction, is to prevent the mitochondrial release of factors controlling activation of caspases and thus the irreversible commitment to undergoing apoptosis (Jacobs and Marnett, 2009).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: The maternal bias of Bag3 substantially increases from P8 to P60.
source: Our RNA-seq analysis of the cerebellum revealed that the maternal bias of Bag3 substantially increases from P8 to P60 whereas Bcl-xL shows a substantial decrease in paternal bias between these two time points (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bcl-xL shows a substantial decrease in paternal bias between P8 and P60.
source: Our RNA-seq analysis of the cerebellum revealed that the maternal bias of Bag3 substantially increases from P8 to P60 whereas Bcl-xL shows a substantial decrease in paternal bias between these two time points (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The parental biases of Bag3 and Bcl-xL are significantly anti-correlated (Pearson correlation coefficient = −0.56; p-value = 0.04) across 16 regions of the adult brain.
source: Further quantification of parental biases across 16 regions of the adult brain (Figure 8B) shows that, with the exception of the ventral midbrain and pons, the parental biases of Bag3 and Bcl-xL are significantly anti-correlated (Pearson correlation coefficient = −0.56; p-value = 0.04, Figure 8B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion had a approximately 15% reduced brain weight compared to wild type littermate controls.
source: However, we found that mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion had a ∼15% reduced brain weight compared to wild type (WT) littermate controls, which carried the Nestin::Cre transgene and two WT copies of Bcl-x (Figure 8D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8D.

claim: Mice with a maternal Bcl-x deletion exhibited no significant difference in brain weight compared to WT littermates.
source: In contrast, mice with a maternal Bcl-x deletion exhibited no significant difference in brain weight compared to WT littermates.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the findings.

claim: Significant differences in area were observed between mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion and both mice with a maternal deletion and WT littermates in cortex, olfactory bulb, and cerebellum.
source: In all three structures, significant differences in area were observed between mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion and both mice with a maternal deletion and WT littermates, while no significant differences were found between mice with a maternal Bcl-x deletion and WT littermates (Figure 8E,F, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8E,F, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: No significant differences in area were found between mice with a maternal Bcl-x deletion and WT littermates in cortex, olfactory bulb, and cerebellum.
source: In all three structures, significant differences in area were observed between mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion and both mice with a maternal deletion and WT littermates, while no significant differences were found between mice with a maternal Bcl-x deletion and WT littermates (Figure 8E,F, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8E,F, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The paternal allele of Bcl-x makes a more substantial contribution to brain development than the maternal allele.
source: Taken together, these results support the hypothesis that the paternal allele of Bcl-x makes a more substantial contribution to brain development than the maternal allele.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: DAPI+, NEUN+, and Vglut1+ cells were significantly reduced in paternal Bcl-x deletion cortices compared to their maternal deletion and WT counterparts.
source: Our data show that DAPI+, NEUN+, and Vglut1+ cells were significantly reduced in paternal Bcl-x deletion cortices compared to their maternal deletion and WT counterparts, while S100ß+ and Gad1+ cells were not significantly affected (Figure 8G,H, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8G,H, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: S100ß+ and Gad1+ cells were not significantly affected by paternal Bcl-x deletion in the cortex.
source: Our data show that DAPI+, NEUN+, and Vglut1+ cells were significantly reduced in paternal Bcl-x deletion cortices compared to their maternal deletion and WT counterparts, while S100ß+ and Gad1+ cells were not significantly affected (Figure 8G,H, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8G,H, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Gad1+ neurons were significantly reduced in number in mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion compared to WT littermates within the molecular and Purkinje layers of the cerebellum.
source: Within the molecular and Purkinje layers, Gad1+ neurons were significantly reduced in number in mice with a paternal Bcl-x deletion compared to WT littermates (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: Stated in the results section with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: Deletion of the paternal allele of Bcl-x causes dramatic reductions in brain size and cell number that are not observed upon deletion of the maternal allele.
source: Together, these results reveal that deletion of the paternal allele of Bcl-x causes dramatic reductions in brain size and cell number that are not observed upon deletion of the maternal allele.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The effects of paternal Bcl-x deletion differ according to cell type and brain region, with specific cell types affected in a given region.
source: Moreover, these effects differ according to cell type and brain region, with specific cell types affected in a given region.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Genomic imprinting plays a role in the regulation of the distribution of specific cell types in distinct areas of the mouse brain.
source: They therefore suggest a largely unexpected role of genomic imprinting in the regulation of the distribution of specific cell types in distinct areas of the mouse brain.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.
